pages.title: Start here: how this workspace runs

text.text: A ten-minute tour of the center in this workspace. Share it with the director, every tutor and whoever answers the phone.
: each student's grade, subject, school, goal, parent contact, tutor and missed sessions.
: the schedule, each linked to a student, tutor and the package it draws from.
: what each family bought, hours used, hours left, paid and expiry.
: diagnostics, practice tests and report cards with goal scores.
: the tutor's note after each session.
Monday: the week's sessions confirmed by text.
Every day: tutors mark sessions and write notes the same evening.
Thursday: packages low on hours or near expiry get a renewal call.
Friday: the director reads the Dashboard: hours by tutor, packages running low, assessments booked.
Every morning: today's sessions and assessments
Every week: progress notes written, missed sessions followed up
Every four weeks: a parent summary and a retest for each student
Every season: tutor schedules and new inquiries for the next term
The director owns intake, plans, packages and parents. Tutors own sessions, notes and assessments. The front desk confirms sessions and chases payment.

Parents pay for progress they can see. Every four weeks each family gets a short summary built from the progress notes and the latest assessment: what improved, what is next, and how many hours are left in the package. Good news goes out by text the same day.
Students appear by first name and last initial. Keep report cards and school records in the family's file, not in notes.
Rename subjects, tests and package sizes and delete the sample rows once your own are in. Edit any cell in place; hours used and left update by themselves.
The center at a glance. Charts read the live tables.

text.text: Families come to a tutoring center worried. The first call and the first session should leave them with a clear plan, a number to beat and a tutor their child likes.
with grade, subject, school and the parent's name and contact.
Ask what is happening at school, in the parent's words, and write the
as something you can measure: "grade-level fractions by spring", "SAT 1350 by March".
Math and reading: a short placement test at grade level and one below.
Test prep: a full timed practice test, so the baseline is honest.

Meet the parent for fifteen minutes after the diagnostic. Show two strengths and two gaps, recommend sessions per week and a package size, and name the tutor. Most students need one or two sessions a week for at least ten weeks to see real change.
The tutor has read the diagnostic and the goal
Start with something the student can do, then one new thing
End with a two-line note to the parent: what we did, what to practice
Book the next eight sessions before they leave

Match on subject first, then on personality. A quiet ninth grader may open up with a calm tutor; a restless fourth grader may need games and movement. Change tutors early and without fuss if it is not working.

A parent calls about her sixth grader's fractions. The director logs the goal, books a diagnostic for Thursday (score 42 out of 80), and recommends a 20-hour package twice a week with the math tutor. Twelve weeks later the retest shows 68 and the report card moves from a C to a B.
Prepaid packages keep scheduling steady and cash predictable. Clear rules, written down and shared before the first payment, prevent nearly every billing argument.
10 hours for single-subject help or a short push before exams.
20 hours for a semester of steady support.
Prices are on each package. Packages are paid before the first session; tick
Every session is linked to the student's active package.
counts sessions that were held, plus sessions missed without notice.
on every session that uses hours.
Cancelled 24 hours or more ahead: no charge, rebook the time.
Cancelled late or missed: the hour is used. The director may waive one per package for illness.
If the tutor cancels, the hour is never charged.

Packages expire after six months (test-prep packs on the test date). A week before expiry, call the family to book the remaining hours. Expired hours are not refunded but may be moved once to a sibling.
When a package has three hours left, the tutor mentions it and the office sends the renewal. Families who renew before the last session keep their time slot.
Unused hours on an active package are refunded at the hourly rate the family paid, less any discount they received for buying in bulk. Mark the package
Dashboard: active packages with fewer than three hours left
Packages expiring in the next two weeks
Sessions marked missed: was the family told the hour was used?

Bao's 30-hour SAT pack has 4.5 hours left and expires in two weeks, the day of his test. The office calls his parents, books three sessions before the test, and offers a short follow-up pack for the second sitting.
Tutors are the product. These are the habits that make a session worth what a family pays for it.
Have the materials ready: a warm-up, the main work, and a short check at the end.
Arrive five minutes early. Families notice.
Warm up with something the student can do (five minutes).
Teach one new idea, then practice it together, then alone.
Check with two or three questions that show whether it stuck.
Leave three minutes for questions about schoolwork.
Students should talk and write more than the tutor. If you are talking most of the hour, change the plan.
Write a progress note: what we covered, the level (needs support, getting there, on track, ahead), what to practice
Tell the office about anything worrying: a sudden drop, a student who seems unhappy
Write a short summary for the parent and book a retest in
. Parents renew when they see progress in numbers.
With the parent's permission, ask the classroom teacher what is coming next. Pre-teaching next week's topic is often the fastest win.
Sessions with minors happen in open rooms or with the door open; online sessions are recorded where families agree.
No private texts with students; messages go through the parent.
Never do a student's homework for them. Show the method, then let them do it.

Calista's note from last week says she is getting there with two-syllable words. The tutor warms up with word cards she knows, introduces a new vowel pattern, reads a short story together, then checks with five new words. Calista reads four; the note says so, and suggests five minutes of reading aloud at home each night.
